analysis.one_liner: Lets governors veto endangered-species listings and hand states control over species found within one state.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in November 2013, received no cosponsors, and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so that no species could be listed as endangered or threatened without the consent of every governor whose state the species lives in, and no listing would take effect unless Congress passed a joint resolution approving it. Every approved listing would expire automatically after five years. It would let governors take over federal protection of species found only in their state, with no court able to review their decisions. It would also guarantee landowners an answer within 90 days on whether a planned use of their property violates the act, treat silence as a yes, pay landowners 150% of their property's value if an agency action cuts its value by half or more, and strip attorney fees from citizen lawsuits brought to enforce the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and developers of land that hosts endangered species habitat, who would gain near-certain approval for planned uses, protection from enforcement actions if an agency misses a 90-day deadline, and compensation well above market value when restrictions do apply. Governors of species-hosting states would gain veto power over federal listings and authority over any species found only within their borders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landowners and developers with restricted property

how_it_helps.text: Owners or lessees could submit any proposed use of their land for a determination within 90 days, and if the Interior Department failed to answer in time, the use would be deemed compliant and shielded as an affirmative defense to civil penalties or prosecution [S2] [S3].

If the Interior Department determined a proposed use violated the act and a Fish and Wildlife Service action cut the property's fair market value by at least 50% for its intended use, the owner or lessee could collect compensation equal to 150% of the property's fair market value, with the government covering appraisal costs [S2] [S3].

Governors could claim exclusive authority over the management of any species they determined existed only within their state, including regulating critical habitat, issuing permits, and setting recovery goals, and those decisions could not be reviewed by any federal or state court [S2] [S3].

Federal hydropower administrators would have to show customers on their monthly bills the share of costs each customer bears from Endangered Species Act compliance, including foregone power generation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public. Species that need federal protection could go unlisted if a governor or Congress withheld approval, and every listing would lapse after five years unless reapproved, raising the risk of extinction, which is irreversible. Taxpayers would fund the 150% compensation payouts and the costs of the compliance-determination program, and citizens would have a harder time enforcing the law in court because attorney fees in citizen suits would be eliminated.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, taxpayers, and imperiled species

drawbacks.text: Requiring the consent of every governor in a species' range, plus approval by a joint resolution of Congress before any listing takes effect [S2], would let a single officeholder block protection for a species, and political species would likely never be listed at all.

Every species on an approved list would be automatically removed five years after enactment unless Congress passed a new joint resolution to relist it [S2] [S3], putting protection on a countdown timer and requiring repeated congressional action just to maintain the status quo.

The 150% compensation requirement, triggered when an agency action cuts a property's value for its intended use by half or more [S3], would expose taxpayers to large payouts above full market value and could make agencies reluctant to designate habitat at all.

A governor's decision to take over a species' management could not be reviewed by any court [S2] [S3], removing the usual check on state officials, and eliminating attorney fee awards in citizen suits [S2] would make it harder for ordinary citizens to afford enforcing the act.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is real: the act's findings note that fewer than 1% of listed species have recovered and been delisted, that landowners effectively bear conservation costs for habitat on their property, and that there is no comprehensive accounting of the act's costs [S3]. Landowner certainty through a guaranteed 90-day determination is a legitimate idea, but this bill pairs it with provisions, like automatic delisting and above-market compensation, that go well past fixing that problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The landowner-certainty idea has genuine merit and addresses a real complaint about the current law. But the bill bundles it with provisions that would dismantle the federal listing system: a gubernatorial veto, a congressional approval requirement, five-year automatic expiration of every listing, unreviewable state takeover of intrastate species, taxpayer-funded payouts at 150% of value, and no attorney fees for citizen enforcers. On balance, the costs to species protection and to taxpayers outweigh the certainty benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Amodei introduced the Endangered Species Management Self-Determination Act on November 19, 2013 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S5].
The action history shows no further activity after referral; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing Endangered Species Act protections stayed fully in place. The bill's prospective beneficiaries—landowners and developers hoping for deemed compliance and 150% compensation—gained nothing, because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Species protections; the bill's beneficiaries gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Mark E. Amodei
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 19, 2013; it attracted no cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources (Chair Doc Hastings)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup after referral, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Republican, ever supported the bill on the record: it had zero cosponsors and no votes were ever taken, so no party breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Landowners and real estate developers with ESA-restricted property
industries.note: The bill would give them guaranteed agency determinations, deemed compliance on missed deadlines, and compensation at 150% of market value. Their gain comes from weaker species protection and payouts funded by taxpayers.

Governor veto power over listings and state takeover of intrastate species would lighten restrictions on grazing and farming on land that hosts listed species, at the cost of recovery chances for those species.

The bill would require federal power marketing administrations to itemize Endangered Species Act compliance costs on customer bills, adding scrutiny, while the bill's overall weakening of listings would reduce their future compliance obligations.

Eliminating attorney fees in citizen suits and removing the petition rulemaking process would cut off the main tools these groups use to enforce the act and compel listings, to the public's detriment in species protection.
